Their metabolism is almost unimaginably slow: some cells may divide once a century, or once a millennium, subsisting on energy fluxes millions of times lower than surface microbes require, hovering at the thermodynamic edge of death. Individual organisms may be thousands of years old, repairing their molecules rather than reproducing, effectively living in geologic time. Collectively, this deep biosphere may harbor a substantial fraction of all bacterial biomass on Earth—an invisible empire beneath the continents and seafloor. It suggests that life needs neither sun nor surface, only rock, water, and chemical disequilibrium—a revelation that makes the subsurface of Mars or Europa's ocean floor seem suddenly, plausibly, alive.
